project_scope.note: Teach the one-carpel legume thread first, then show the family's extreme flower and leaf diversity.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Find the fruit or ovary first. A single superior carpel becoming a legume or modified legume is the strongest thread through the family.
family_diagnostics.leaves: Usually alternate and stipulate; leaves may be simple, trifoliolate, pinnate, palmately compound or bipinnate. Pulvini are common.
family_diagnostics.flowers: Flower architecture ranges from papilionoid pea flowers to caesalpinioid-like and mimosoid forms.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Usually a legume from one carpel, but it may be dehiscent, indehiscent, flattened, segmented, winged or otherwise modified.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Do not require a pea flower. Use stipules/pulvini as supporting characters and let the one-carpel fruit do the heavy lifting.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: mature legume → bipinnate leaf → redbud pea flower → huisache mimosoid flower → Dalea tiny-flowered spikes and silky leaflets → seed and pod variation → missing true leaf-base and carpel anatomy macros
visual_lesson.intro: A real legume can have flowers that resemble peas, redbuds, tiny prairie clovers, or mimosoid puffballs. Learn the single-carpel fruit, pinnate and bipinnate leaves, banner/wing/keel flower parts, then follow each type to its pods. Newly verified Astragalus photos show both a slender curved legume and a thick fleshy one; those do not all prove the same species.

steps.title: 1 · Follow one flower to a legume pod
steps.look_for: Multiple individual curved PODS from Illinois bundleflower; each pod encloses seeds. This photographed cluster has pods opened and curled, not one giant round fruit.
steps.why_it_matters: A pod derived from one carpel is the main family thread even when its shape is unusual. This is an actual installed JPEG.

steps.title: 2 · Understand a bipinnate leaf
steps.look_for: On this exact-species sharp-pod bundleflower photograph, find the main leaf axis, its side PINNAE and the tiny paired LEAFLETS. This is a leaf architecture common in mimosoid-type legumes, not all Fabaceae.
steps.why_it_matters: Prevents confusing an entire leaf with one pinna, and shows why the pea family can have almost fernlike foliage.

steps.title: 3 · See a pea-type flower, not a puffball
steps.look_for: Texas redbud has clusters of pink individual pea-like flowers directly on older branches. Their banner, wing and keel petal groups require a closer single-flower macro to point out individually.
steps.why_it_matters: One member of Fabaceae has pea-style (papilionoid) flowers, unlike mimosoid flower heads.

steps.title: 4 · Contrast a mimosoid-type flower head
steps.look_for: Huisache's yellow sphere is a cluster of many tiny individual flowers. The long yellow stamens give the puffball appearance; separate green bipinnate leaves appear on the same twig.
steps.why_it_matters: The legume family is not limited to pink pea flowers; show the small-flower mimosoid pattern.

steps.title: 5 · Dalea prairie clover: a flowering spike, not a puffball
steps.photo_role: dense prairie clover inflorescence / tiny papilionoid flowers
steps.look_for: Look at this WHITE PRAIRIE CLOVER flowering head: it is a cylindrical spike of many individual WHITE flowers, not a single flower and not a mimosoid sphere dominated by long stamens. The tiny petals have an irregular pea-relative floral plan, but their banner/wings/keel positions require a detached-flower macro.
steps.why_it_matters: Shows a third familiar Fabaceae appearance beyond redbud pea flowers and huisache mimosoid puffs, while reinforcing what an inflorescence is.

steps.title: 6 · Golden prairie clover: silky leaves and a fuzzy head
steps.photo_role: silky leaflets / densely hairy flower spike
steps.look_for: Find the whitish SILKY HAIRS around the dense head and the divided foliage (each small blade is a LEAFLET). A prairie-clover plant can be very hairy without resembling a bean, yet its reproductive system still belongs in the legume family. This is a texture/habit reference, not a verified fruit pod close-up.
steps.why_it_matters: Shows botanical hair terminology (silky, villous), fine leaflet architecture and the need to confirm tiny Fabaceae pods separately.

steps.title: 11 · Learn a milkvetch's true pea flower
steps.photo_role: Astragalus pinnate leaf / banner wing keel / narrow pod
steps.image_label: Smallflower milkvetch in Texas, pea flowers and pods
steps.look_for: In this real Texas photo, find one conspicuous upper BANNER petal, two lateral WINGS and the lower KEEL; then follow the slender stem to the multi-leaflet PINNATE leaves and curved legume below the blossoms.
steps.why_it_matters: Shows the papilionoid flower form in a REAL milkvetch, and how its one-carpel pod differs from mimosoid flower heads.

steps.title: 12 · See a plump legume that isn't a bean pod
steps.photo_role: hairy fleshy milkvetch pod / pubescence and seam
steps.image_label: Platte River milkvetch green fleshy pods
steps.image_credit: Chet Burrier · CC BY (per canonical photo)
steps.look_for: Two fat, green, slightly fuzzy pods—both are true FABACEAE legumes. A groundplum look-alike also makes plump fruit; examine ovary HAIRS and mature seams to separate the actual Astragalus species.
steps.why_it_matters: Teaches that a legume need not be long, flat or immediately bean-shaped. Species differences may need fruit hair and groove macros.

steps.title: 13 · Contrast a long thin Astragalus pod
steps.photo_role: long narrow pointed milkvetch pods / leaflets
steps.look_for: Many long, slim, mostly straight pods stick out from very thin stems. Compare this exact-species image with the thick, fleshy green fruits of A. plattensis. Both are TRUE legume fruits; a legume need not look like a broad bean pod.
steps.why_it_matters: One family making dramatically different pods is an essential visual correction—fruit form can identify some genera and species even without flowers.

steps.title: 5 · Look at an individual legume seed
steps.look_for: Five dark small Illinois bundleflower seeds, with a printed 2-mm scale. This is what an individual mature seed can look like after a legume opens.
steps.why_it_matters: Connects the seed to its former enclosure inside the pod. Not every Fabaceae seed has this size or appearance.

steps.title: 6 · Compare another pod shape
steps.look_for: Prairie bundleflower has long, slender brown pods instead of a compact curled bundle. A hand provides approximate scale (not a calibrated ruler).
steps.why_it_matters: Demonstrates that legumes can look very different even inside one genus.

steps.title: 7 · Find stipules and swollen leaf joints
steps.look_for: Find the small stipule at the leaf stalk base and the swollen PULVINUS joint. We need a verified real macro, so the image is intentionally blank instead of reusing a misleading leaf photo.
steps.why_it_matters: Supporting leaf-base characters are widespread in Fabaceae but not universally obvious in every species.

steps.title: 8 · Follow the single carpel to fruit
steps.photo_role: single carpel and superior ovary dissection
steps.look_for: Dissect an actual Fabaceae flower to reveal one carpel; follow it to a mature pod and its seams. We do not have a licensed, clearly verified macro sequence for this part yet.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the reproductive origin of a true legume, independent of whether flowers are pea-like or mimosoid.

comparisons.title: Fabaceae vs Rosaceae
comparisons.rule: Both can have stipules and compound leaves. Fabaceae centers on one superior carpel becoming a legume; Rosaceae commonly uses a hypanthium and different fruit architectures.

comparisons.title: Modern classification
comparisons.rule: Use papilionoid, caesalpinioid-like and mimosoid as flower architectures. Do not teach the old three-group shorthand as the modern formal subfamily system.

comparisons.title: Mesquite (Neltuma) versus huisache (Vachellia)
comparisons.rule: Mesquite: long creamy cylindrical flower SPIKES and long often straw-colored pods. Huisache: round golden flower HEADS and shorter, hard, swollen dark pods; inspect bipinnate leaf and node armature.

comparisons.title: Huisache versus whitethorn
comparisons.rule: Both can have paired straight nodal stipular SPINES and golden flower balls. Mature whitethorn pods are long, slim and often constricted between seeds; huisache pods are stout and hard.

comparisons.title: Catclaw (Senegalia) versus Vachellia
comparisons.rule: Senegalia commonly bears recurved PRICKLES on stems; Vachellia typically has paired STRAIGHT STIPULAR SPINES at a leaf node. Compare thorn attachment, not color alone.

comparisons.title: Prairie acacia (Acaciella) versus thorny relatives
comparisons.rule: Local prairie acacia has fine bipinnate leaves and pale/cream globose heads but lacks the hooked prickles or prominent paired straight spines of the thorny woody acacias; no local species card installed yet.

comparisons.title: Bundleflower Desmanthus vs Mimosa and Neptunia
comparisons.rule: Unarmed mostly herbaceous Desmanthus has bipinnate leaves with a raised petiolar/rachis gland near the proximal pinnae; pod length/width, flower count and stamen number separate its species. Compare whole node for Mimosa (often prickly) or Neptunia (yellow puffs); leaf folding alone is not diagnostic.

comparisons.title: Dalea tiny-flowered spikes vs Vachellia staminal heads
comparisons.rule: Dalea has small modified irregular pea-related florets in elongated/dense flower spikes; Vachellia yellow balls are made from tiny mimosoid flowers whose long numerous stamens create the puff. Do not equate any flower cluster with one giant flower.

comparisons.title: Astragalus vs Desmanthus / Mimosa
comparisons.rule: Astragalus often shows obvious bilateral pea flowers and pinnate leaves with numerous leaflets; Desmanthus and Mimosa have bipinnate foliage and globose many-flowered heads. Mature fruit and actual leaf branching are the most reliable clues.

comparisons.title: Groundplum vs slim milkvetch pod
comparisons.rule: Within Astragalus, both narrow dry pods and fleshy plum-like pods come from one carpel. Among plump fruit types, hair and seam grooves (A. plattensis versus A. crassicarpus var. berlandieri) may be more useful than overall pod size.

visual_lesson.caveat: Family example photos deliberately represent different genera. Never claim ALL Fabaceae are bipinnate or puffball-flowered. The family can have papilionoid, caesalpinioid-like and mimosoid flower architectures, with many modified pods; photographic examples are unannotated and species-labeled. New Dalea examples are species-labeled real physically installed photographs. They show spike texture and leaflet context, not detached tiny petals or a verified calyx/legume fruit. Color, hair and flower arrangement are not all-family diagnostic traits. Astragalus family examples use physically installed taxon-labeled photos. A. lindheimeri has CC BY-NC restrictions and the two zero-photo varieties are NOT represented by nonmatching 'similar' variety images. Macro arrows are pending original-image verification. A. leptocarpus now has a licensed physically installed CC BY 2.0 exact-species pod photo; faint small pod seams require a separate scaled macro.

previous_steps_20261013.look_for: A fruit derived from one superior carpel, even when the pod is tiny or indehiscent.
previous_steps_20261013.why_it_matters: The one-carpel fruit is the safest structural thread across Fabaceae diversity.

previous_steps_20261013.title: 2 · Check the leaf base
previous_steps_20261013.look_for: Stipules and a slightly swollen pulvinus at the petiole or leaflet base.
previous_steps_20261013.why_it_matters: These support the family ID even when flower shape is unfamiliar.

previous_steps_20261013.title: 3 · Learn the pea architecture
previous_steps_20261013.look_for: Banner/standard, wings and keel—or a modified version of that plan.
previous_steps_20261013.why_it_matters: Papilionoid architecture is common, but it is one branch of family diversity.

previous_steps_20261013.title: 4 · Expect exceptions
previous_steps_20261013.look_for: Tiny specialized flowers that do not resemble a garden pea at first glance.
previous_steps_20261013.why_it_matters: Prevents the learner from rejecting true legumes with nonclassic flowers.

family_confusion_cleanup.field_question: What exact floral or fruit structure confirms this family, and which nearby family could mimic it?
look_here_first: Locate a single superior carpel or mature legume, including modified indehiscent fruits.
At leaf nodes inspect stipules and pulvini; supportive but not universal.
Identify papilionoid, Senna-like or mimosoid reproductive architecture without treating any one as required.

comparison_matrix.separate: Winglike petaloid sepals and a staminal sheath can mimic a pea flower; dissect the perianth and gynoecium rather than equating wings with Fabaceae wing petals.
Both may have stipules and many stamens; Fabaceae has one carpel forming a legume, whereas Rosaceae often has a hypanthium and drupes, pomes or aggregate fruits.
Puffball-like flowers with conspicuous numerous stamens and small petals vs banner/wing/keel architecture; both remain Fabaceae.

genus_routing_cues: Dalea: compact heads/spikes with reduced papilionoid corollas; inspect floral bracts and pod.
Senna: asymmetric flowers, conspicuous anthers, and legume; photograph anther pores/dehiscence.
Mimosa: bipinnate leaves and clustered small flowers with conspicuous stamens; use fruit segments and armature.
Sesbania: pinnate foliage, papilionoid flowers and elongated pods.
